strengths: The paper identifies a real bottleneck for convolutional sequence models: exact autoregressive decoding is less naturally incremental than recurrent SSM decoding, despite efficient FFT-based training/prefill.

The FutureFill idea is simple, clean, and appears technically plausible for single causal convolutional filters: precompute the contribution of the prompt to future positions via one FFT, then account explicitly for newly generated tokens.
The asymptotic improvement in the prompt setting, from roughly O(LK) decode dependence on the prompt to O(L log L + K^2), is potentially useful when K is much smaller than the context length L.
The paper clearly distinguishes generation from a prompt and online prediction, and provides concise algorithms and runtime arguments.
The connection to spectral filtering and online prediction is interesting, and the method preserves exactness rather than relying on distillation or approximation.
weaknesses: The core contribution is quite narrow and somewhat straightforward: it is essentially a shifted convolution precomputation/cache for future prompt contributions. The paper does not convincingly establish that this is novel enough or technically deep enough for a top-tier AI conference.

The claim that the method applies to any convolutional sequence prediction algorithm is under-justified. The paper analyzes a single linear convolutional filter, but modern architectures such as Hyena, gated SSM-style blocks, stacked nonlinear convolutional models, and multi-channel layers require more careful treatment of intermediate activations, nonlinearities, and layer-wise caches.

The experimental evaluation is very limited. It only reports simple CPU timing for one layer in an online synthetic decoding loop, without real language modeling, real convolutional architectures, GPU/accelerator measurements, end-to-end latency, memory measurements, or quality-preserving generation experiments.
The main practical prompt-generation result is not experimentally validated, even though it is the central setting highlighted in the introduction and comparison table.

The runtime presentation contains ambiguities and possible inconsistencies. For example, Algorithm 2 sets K using notation that appears to conflate sqrt(L) log L with sqrt(L log L), while the proof and stated amortized bounds are not fully consistent.

The comparison to attention and standard convolution is incomplete. Attention has different cache semantics and hardware behavior, while convolutional models often have structured recurrent forms or approximations; the paper does not compare against optimized existing inference implementations or recurrent conversions.

Reproducibility is weak: the experiments lack hardware specifications, implementation details, exact model/filter setup, token dimensions, number of trials, variance/error bars, and code availability.
The paper overstates practical impact. The text says inference gains materialize for large models on accelerated hardware, but provides no supporting data, making this an unsupported empirical claim.

The regret/spectral filtering discussion is intriguing but thin. The paper asserts the same regret bound with improved runtime, but does not spell out the full assumptions, update rule correctness, or a formal theorem beyond a brief corollary.
Overall, the work is technically plausible and potentially useful, but the evidence and scope are below what I would expect for acceptance at a top-tier AI venue.

strengths: The paper identifies a real bottleneck for exact autoregressive inference in long-convolution sequence models and focuses on an important efficiency question.
The core idea of precomputing future convolution contributions from the prompt/cache is simple and potentially useful for implementations where exact convolutional decoding is needed.

The asymptotic claims are presented clearly at a high level, and the paper attempts to connect the method to several convolutional architectures, including STU, Hyena-style models, and SSM-related convolutional views.
weaknesses: The contribution appears quite limited and close to a straightforward blocked/FFT caching observation. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish FutureFill from standard overlap-save/block convolution, streaming convolution, or other classical FFT-based online convolution techniques.

There are significant technical inconsistencies in the formal setup. The model is first defined with context length L and filter phi in R^L, but Algorithm 1 takes phi in R^{L+K} and computes predictions using sums up to t. This changes the effective context and makes the claimed comparison to fixed-context convolution unclear.

Algorithm 2 seems incomplete or incorrect as written: the cache is used before being initialized for the first block, and the block size notation K = sqrt(L log L) is ambiguous relative to the stated O(sqrt(L) log L) rate. These issues weaken confidence in the main online-generation theorem.

The STU case study is not technically convincing. Algorithm 3 appears to use invalid cache indices at initialization and gives an incorrect-looking update M^{t+1} <- gradient loss rather than a standard online gradient update. The claim of preserving the same regret bound is essentially asserted rather than proved carefully.

The claim that the method applies to any convolutional model is overstated. Multi-channel filters, nonlinearities, gating, Hyena-style nested products, and full model inference costs are only discussed informally; the analysis is for a simple linear convolution and does not rigorously cover the broader architectures highlighted in the motivation.

The empirical evaluation is very weak for a top-tier AI venue. It uses only a synthetic/single-layer CPU timing experiment, omits implementation details, lacks comparisons to optimized baselines or classical streaming FFT convolution, and does not evaluate real language/model workloads or GPU inference.

The paper does not provide enough evidence that the asymptotic speedups translate into practical gains. The discussion explicitly avoids optimized inference settings, which are exactly where the contribution would need to matter.
Reproducibility is limited: the experimental setup, hardware, model dimensions, code availability, and exact timing methodology are not specified in sufficient detail.

Positioning is incomplete. The paper cites recent convolutional sequence models but does not engage deeply with the broader signal-processing and systems literature on fast online convolution, block FFT methods, and cache-efficient decoding.

Overall, while the idea may be useful as an implementation trick, the current manuscript has unresolved correctness/clarity issues and far too little empirical support for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper identifies a clean and important computational problem: exact autoregressive generation for convolutional sequence models, where naive decoding loses the FFT advantage enjoyed during training/prefill.
The core FutureFill idea is simple, intuitive, and potentially useful: precompute future prompt contributions with an FFT cache, then add the contribution from newly generated tokens online.
The asymptotic analyses for the main prefill and online settings are easy to follow and, at a high level, support meaningful improvements over naive exact convolutional decoding.
The paper is concise and well motivated by current interest in long convolutional models, SSMs, STUs, and Hyena-like architectures.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is much too limited for a top-tier acceptance: it appears to be a single-layer CPU synthetic timing experiment, with no real model, no language/modeling task, no GPU or inference-stack measurements, no memory measurements, and no comparison to optimized convolutional, recurrent/SSM, or hybrid implementations.

Several claims are broader than what is demonstrated. The paper says the method applies to any convolutional model, including models with multiple channels, nonlinearities, and Hyena-style composition, but the formal development is essentially for a single linear convolution filter; the extension to nonlinear multi-layer architectures is asserted rather than carefully specified or evaluated.

There are important clarity and consistency issues in the setup. The paper defines a context length L with phi in R^L, but Algorithm 1 uses phi in R^{L+K} and sums to t=L+tau, which makes the exact relationship between fixed-context decoding and growing-context decoding ambiguous.

The novelty may be viewed as incremental: the method is essentially blockwise FFT precomputation/caching for convolutional autoregression. The paper would need stronger positioning against known overlap-save/overlap-add streaming convolution and block convolution methods to establish that the contribution is not a straightforward adaptation.

The online algorithm and STU case study are underdeveloped. Algorithm 2 does not clearly initialize the cache for early iterations, the choice of K is notationally ambiguous, and Algorithm 3 contains what appears to be an incorrect update rule, setting parameters to a gradient rather than taking an optimization step.

The comparison to attention is somewhat unfair or underspecified: exact attention has different data dependencies and cache behavior, but the paper does not compare against practical KV caching regimes or clarify when its asymptotic cache advantage translates into wall-clock or memory advantage in realistic deployments.

Reproducibility is weak. The experiment lacks enough implementation detail, hardware information, code availability, numerical correctness checks, and variance/error reporting to independently assess the claimed speedups.

strengths: The paper identifies an important practical bottleneck for long convolutional sequence models: exact autoregressive decoding is much slower than training-time FFT convolution and has unfavorable prompt-cache behavior.

The FutureFill primitive is simple, intuitive, and technically useful. The paper gives clear algorithms with meaningful asymptotic improvements: O(L log^2 L) exact online convolution and O(L log L + K log^2 K) prompted generation with O(K) cache.
The work offers a useful compute-memory tradeoff via Epoched-FutureFill, which appears more practical than the full O(L)-memory continuous version and is validated with a cache-length sweep.

Empirical results on controlled convolutions and academic-scale FlashSTU-T variants support the expected subquadratic scaling, with nontrivial speedups at long generation lengths and large prompt lengths.
weaknesses: Novelty is weakened substantially by the acknowledged independent work on Flash Inference, which reportedly achieves the same O(L log^2 L) asymptotic result. The paper does not compare experimentally against that method, so the claimed practical advantage of FutureFill/Epoched-FutureFill remains under-supported.

The end-to-end empirical gains are moderate and regime-dependent. FutureFill is often slower than the naive baseline at shorter lengths, and the headline speedups are around 1.5x-2x only for large sequences or long prompts, which makes the practical impact less decisive.

The experimental setup is limited for language modeling claims: the convolutional language models use randomly initialized filters and the paper focuses only on speed, with no evaluation of generation quality, trained models, perplexity, or downstream utility. This makes it hard to judge whether the method benefits realistic deployed convolutional LMs.

Baselines are incomplete. The main comparisons are against naive online convolution and standard attention/KV cache, but not against optimized exact/near-exact convolution inference systems, the closely related Flash Inference work, recurrent/SSM conversions, or more hardware-aware implementations.

The claim of applicability to any convolutional model is broader than what is formally shown. The theory is developed for linear convolution, while modern architectures include nonlinearities, gating, layer interactions, hybrid attention, and implementation details that are only sketched rather than rigorously analyzed.

Reproducibility is not fully convincing. The paper describes implementation details and uses public components, but it is unclear whether the authors' FutureFill implementation, benchmarking harness, and exact configurations are released. Timing is averaged over only two post-warmup runs, giving weak statistical evidence.

Some presentation and technical details need tightening: Algorithm 2 appears to omit the k=0 case for odd timesteps, there are typographical issues in tables and proofs, and several extracted equations/proof lines are hard to parse. These do not necessarily invalidate the idea, but they reduce confidence in polish and rigor.

strengths: The core problem is important for convolutional sequence models: exact autoregressive decoding has a quadratic bottleneck, and reducing this without approximation is a meaningful goal.
The FutureFill abstraction is simple and intuitive, and the paper gives clean algorithms for both a practical memory/runtime tradeoff and a quasilinear-time online convolution procedure.
The asymptotic claims are mostly well motivated, and the prompt-generation setting addresses a practically relevant cache-size issue for long-context inference.
The paper includes controlled experiments and larger model-timing experiments, including ablations over generation length, model size, prefill length, and cache length K.
weaknesses: The novelty is weakened substantially by the cited independent work that obtains the same O(L log^2 L) runtime. The paper argues that FutureFill is simpler and enables practical variants, but this distinction is not developed enough to make the contribution clearly strong.

The empirical evaluation is disappointing for the claimed practical impact. The main model experiments use randomly initialized filters/models and focus only on timing, so they do not demonstrate usefulness on trained convolutional language models or realistic generation workloads.

The realized speedups are modest relative to the theoretical improvement: about 1.5-1.7x without prefill and around 2x in selected prefill settings. This raises questions about whether the method is practically compelling on modern hardware.

The baseline story is narrow. The main comparisons are against naive online convolution; the paper does not compare to the independent Flash Inference approach, optimized chunked/streaming convolution implementations, approximate recurrent distillations, or other practical inference systems for long convolution models.

Memory accounting is not fully satisfying. The algorithms often count only additional cache memory while excluding storage of generated inputs/activations and filters, and the paper does not report peak GPU memory in experiments despite making cache-size claims.

The experiments have weak statistical support: timings average only two post-warmup runs, several tables contain apparent formatting or numerical errors, and there is little discussion of hardware sensitivity or implementation overhead.

The theoretical presentation has some rough edges and apparent typos in proofs and tables, which do not necessarily invalidate the method but reduce confidence in the polish and care of the submission.

Overall, the paper is technically plausible and contains a useful idea, but the combination of limited novelty, weak practical evaluation, narrow baselines, and modest demonstrated gains leaves it slightly below the acceptance threshold for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely bottleneck: exact autoregressive inference for convolutional sequence models, where training-time FFT efficiency does not directly translate to decoding efficiency.

The FutureFill primitive is simple, intuitive, and broadly applicable to convolutional predictors. The presentation makes clear why past generated tokens can be used to precompute their future contributions exactly.

The theoretical results are meaningful: Epoched-FutureFill gives a tunable compute-memory tradeoff, and Continuous-FutureFill reduces exact online convolution from quadratic to quasilinear time with linear additional memory.
The prompt-generation setting is especially compelling, since the claimed O(K) cache independent of prompt length directly addresses a practical long-context inference issue.

The experiments include both controlled convolution benchmarks and reasonably large academic-scale convolutional language model workloads on H100s, with results generally matching the predicted scaling and showing nontrivial speedups.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat weakened by the cited independent concurrent work on near-linear convolutional inference with the same O(L log^2 L) asymptotic runtime. The paper argues FutureFill is simpler and enables practical variants, but the comparison to this closest related work remains mostly qualitative and lacks empirical or technical side-by-side analysis.

The main deep-model experiments evaluate the more practical Epoched-FutureFill, not the headline Continuous-FutureFill quasilinear algorithm. This leaves some uncertainty about the practical value of the strongest theoretical result in realistic model stacks.

The experimental baselines are limited. The primary baseline is naive online convolution, which is a natural reference but not necessarily the strongest exact inference baseline; the paper does not compare against the concurrent flash-inference-style method or other block/FFT-based exact decoding implementations.

The language-model experiments use randomly initialized filters and focus only on speed, so they do not establish behavior for trained models or interactions with generation quality, numerical stability, or real deployment settings.

The cache-size claim for prompt-based generation is theoretically attractive, but the empirical section reports mostly runtime and does not provide direct memory measurements, cache footprint comparisons, or detailed GPU memory profiling.

There are several clarity and polish issues: Algorithm 2 has edge-case ambiguities near sequence boundaries and for k(t) on odd t, the proof of Proposition 1 appears to contain a summation typo, and some appendix tables contain formatting or numeric errors such as malformed entries and apparent outliers.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details are substantial, but the appendix appears to omit a URL for the FlashSTU source line and does not clearly state whether FutureFill code and benchmark scripts will be released.
